title: AI Is the Reactor, Not the Plant
basis: Reconstructed from the complete published index.md and accepted legacy spec.md, using check_draft.py units and outcome_specs.parse_draft on the preserved 2026-11-12 baseline. The article has 29 prose/list units plus its unchanged three-bullet KEY POINTS callout. Tables, images and captions remain evidence attached to their existing units. The contract preserves the seven original body sections and their paragraph counts, moves the existing Questions to Consider unit before Closing Thought, and adds one short final hand-off unit, for 30 specified prose/list units. It requires a fuller roadmap, a bridge from intended behavior to surrounding controls, an explicit non-universal interpretation of the cost evidence, and a closing synthesis. These are prospective requirements, not claims about the unchanged Phase A prose. No journal research ledger exists: the baseline article and legacy spec are the factual authority, including every nuclear cost figure and its qualification. Intent, the five thesis fields and role are copied unchanged from the final journal entry. The author authorized auto mode and no more than two total draft-check rounds; the spec remains draft.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader maps each of control, channel, and contain to a concrete AI practice and explains why a single safeguard is insufficient.
acceptance_criteria.probe: For an AI workflow, what would control, channel, and contain mean, and what does defense in depth add?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Control limits actions through scope, instructions, or permissions; channel turns outputs into checked results through evaluation or workflows; contain bounds failures through sandboxing, review, limits, or rollback; another layer must hold when one fails.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader uses the nuclear evidence directionally and can state the analogy's limits.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What does the nuclear cost evidence support, and what should you avoid inferring about AI from the analogy?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The surrounding plant accounts for substantial work and cost; attributed breakdowns with different bases are not universal ratios or AI budgets; AI has different hazards, changing behavior, and can have value without a production control system.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader identifies an engineering or organizational investment beyond choosing a more capable model.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What concrete change would this article suggest to the staffing, measurement, or ownership of an AI project?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Budget for evaluation and surrounding systems, define permissions and layered safeguards, measure conversion into correct results, or name the accountable human owner; connect the choice to trustworthy use.

thesis.question: Where should teams direct engineering effort when a capable model is already available?
thesis.claim: Teams seeking trustworthy production use should treat the model as one component and direct most engineering effort to the surrounding controls, evaluation, workflows, and accountable operation.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that selecting or training a sufficiently capable model solves most of the production problem, leaving integration and oversight as minor finishing work.
thesis.so_what: Project budgets, delivery plans, and ownership need to include the work that turns a convincing demonstration into a service people can rely on.
thesis.how_why: Raw generation does not itself constrain permitted actions, verify results, contain failures, or assign responsibility; those properties come from the systems around it, as the bounded reactor analogy illustrates.

supporting_claims.claim: A capable core is only one component of a usable system, as the reactor function and attributed plant cost evidence illustrate.
Control, channel and contain identify distinct engineering responsibilities that turn model output into trustworthy production work.
Safeguards need independent layers designed to hold when another layer fails.
Organizations and society need accountable operating structures around capability, extending the plant analogy beyond software.
The reactor analogy supports a bounded argument about surrounding work, without transferring nuclear cost ratios or physical hazards to AI.
Teams should make the surrounding work explicit in project budgets, permissions, measurement and human ownership.

role.contribution: Establishes the engineering controls and ownership for dependable production use, preparing for the later product essay's separate question of changing customer workflows.

additional_patterns.applies_to: reactor-core and plant-cost: explain the heat source, give attributed cost evidence, and interpret it directionally.
three-jobs through widening-out: engineering functions, layered safeguards, then organizational and societal operation.
analogy-limits through monday and questions: constrain the analogy before turning it into planning decisions.

flow.rationale: The reader first learns what the nuclear core supplies and why the surrounding plant accounts for substantial work. Only then can the three jobs and independent safeguards give the AI comparison concrete meaning. Organizations and society extend those already explained responsibilities; their limits are stated before practical advice so the analogy does not become a claim of equivalent hazards or budgets. The Monday moves supply the terms needed by the unchanged team questions. Moving those questions before the closing synthesis keeps application beside action and lets the article finish on the investment decision and its consequence for the next essay. Starting with cost percentages would leave their object unclear; moving the wider analogy before the engineering mapping would leave it ungrounded; putting questions after references would break the closing and leave them outside the specification alignment.

hook.content: It is easy to be dazzled by the core.

bridge.from_reader_world: Engineers can generate structure cheaply and can name intended behavior, yet are still tempted to judge AI work by which model is most capable.
bridge.to_topic: A model alone does not make that intended behavior dependable; the reactor and its surrounding plant distinguish raw capability from the work that controls and checks it.

thesis_statement.text: For trustworthy production use, the model is the reactor; most of the engineering is the plant around it that controls, channels and contains its capability.

sections.heading: What a Reactor Core Actually Is
sections.controlling_idea: A reactor supplies heat whose useful production role depends on control.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the source and the necessary surrounding work before cost evidence or AI mapping depends on those terms.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction distinguishes raw power from a useful plant.
transition_in.introduces: The reactor core as a heat source whose output must be controlled.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A reactor core is the plant’s heat source.

evidence.what: The NRC describes the reactor as the heat source for the power plant, just like the boiler is for a coal plant; the paragraph identifies the self-sustaining fission chain reaction as how that heat is produced.
evidence.shows: The unusual physics does not change the reactor’s limited functional role within the whole plant.
evidence.source: U.S. NRC, Reactor Concepts Manual (R-100), as quoted in the baseline article

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Controlling the chain reaction makes its heat usable for predictable electricity generation.

evidence.what: The existing NRC quotation connects consistent and constant heat energy with predictable and controllable steam generation and electricity.
evidence.shows: Steady useful output is a result of control, not a synonym for raw heat.
evidence.source: U.S. NRC, Reactor Concepts Manual (R-100), as quoted in the baseline article

transition_in.carries_over: The core provides heat.
transition_in.introduces: Why that heat must be steady to serve the plant.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An unchecked reaction illustrates why control is essential to making the heat source usable.

evidence.what: The baseline explains an unchecked reaction producing energy faster than surrounding systems can use or absorb it, and the inability to run a grid on an unsteady source.
evidence.shows: Control is part of the useful system rather than a cosmetic feature. Preserve the existing physical account without introducing detonation language or new nuclear claims.
evidence.source: Baseline index.md, What a Reactor Core Actually Is paragraph 3

transition_in.carries_over: Controlled heat supports predictable generation.
transition_in.introduces: The unusable and dangerous result described for an unchecked reaction.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The core can matter enormously while still requiring the surrounding plant to fulfill its purpose.

evidence.what: The existing core-matters conclusion follows the heat-source and control explanation.
evidence.shows: Valuing the plant does not require dismissing the core, and prepares the reader to ask how much engineering sits around it.

transition_in.carries_over: The contrast between steady output and an unchecked reaction.
transition_in.introduces: The distinction between an essential core and a complete usable system.

flow.rationale: Define the heat source, explain steady use, contrast the unchecked case, and draw the core-versus-system distinction. Reversing the control and hazard paragraphs would introduce the failure before the reader knows the useful operating goal.

sections.heading: Most of the Plant Is Not the Core
sections.controlling_idea: The attributed nuclear estimates show substantial cost outside the reactor without establishing a universal ratio.

advances_thesis.how: Grounds the surrounding-work claim in existing numbers while keeping their source years, bases and limits visible.

transition_in.carries_over: The core needs surrounding engineering to become useful.
transition_in.introduces: Existing cost evidence for the scale of that surrounding work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most of a nuclear plant’s cost and engineering sits outside the reactor.

evidence.what: The baseline article’s directional claim about cost, components and engineering effort leads into its attributed cost breakdowns.
evidence.shows: The numbers are introduced to support a scale-of-work argument rather than a decimal target.
evidence.source: Baseline index.md, Most of the Plant Is Not the Core

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two attributed estimates put the reactor-related share in a minority while using different cost bases.

evidence.what: WNA’s 2020 supply-chain breakdown: nuclear island about 28% of plant cost, already including the reactor coolant system and steam supply; conventional island (turbine) about 15%; balance of plant about 18%; site and civil works about 20%; instrumentation and control about 8%. The vessel and core alone are smaller than the nuclear island.
evidence.shows: Large shares pay for systems around the reactor; the named nuclear-island category must not be mistaken for the bare core.
evidence.source: World Nuclear Association, Economics of Nuclear Power, 2020 supply-chain cost-by-activity breakdown, as cited in the baseline

evidence.what: The 1980 DOE estimate is for a hypothetical plant and is illustrative, not a constant: reactor 15–20% of direct cost, co-equal with turbine and plant structures; engineering design cost nearly as much as the reactor; roughly a third of total cost was indirect services, construction management and overhead.
evidence.shows: A separately based historical estimate points in the same direction. Its direct-cost denominator differs from the WNA percentages, so the estimates cannot be treated as strictly comparable.
evidence.source: IFP, Why Does Nuclear Power Plant Construction Cost So Much?, reporting the 1980 DOE breakdown, as cited in the baseline

evidence.what: The unchanged intuition/reality table contrasts equating reactor and plant, treating the core as the hard part, and assuming a better core alone makes a better plant.
evidence.shows: The cost figures support redirecting attention toward control, cooling, containment, instrumentation and conversion rather than treating the source as the whole system.

transition_in.carries_over: The surrounding plant carries much of the work.
transition_in.introduces: The attributed WNA and historical DOE figures, with their qualifications kept beside them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The cost evidence is directional support for surrounding work, not a universal reactor percentage or an AI budget formula.

evidence.what: Unchanged Figure 1 and its plant-cost-breakdown.jpeg image and caption reproduce the WNA 2020 cost-by-activity comparison, including the nuclear-island label and about 28% share.
evidence.shows: The visual reinforces the minority share of the named nuclear-island category; the paragraph and preceding list carry the definitions and caveats needed to read it.

transition_in.carries_over: The two sources point the same way despite different bases.
transition_in.introduces: The bounded inference the article draws from those figures.

flow.rationale: State the surrounding-work claim, present the complete attributed list with its caveats and contrast table, then give the directional interpretation beside the figure. Moving the interpretation away from the numbers would make a false precise comparison easier.

transition_in.carries_over: The table and figure show three jobs around the core.
transition_in.introduces: Their shared focus on useful, trustworthy operation rather than more raw power.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The surrounding controls create trust by making generated work inspectable and testable.

sections.heading: Defense in Depth: No Single Guardrail
sections.controlling_idea: A safeguard must be backed by independent layers that can hold when it fails.

advances_thesis.how: Develops containment and control from a list of measures into a design principle about failure.

transition_in.carries_over: The surrounding controls are where trustworthy operation is built.
transition_in.introduces: Why those controls cannot depend on a single guardrail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Trust in the surrounding controls requires a plan for a safeguard failing.

evidence.what: The existing transition introduces one more nuclear idea; make its connection to the preceding trust claim explicit without adding another unit.
evidence.shows: The reader knows why independent layers follow the three-job mapping rather than reading the section as a new analogy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Nuclear defense in depth assumes failures and supplies successive independent protections.

evidence.what: Preserve the IAEA’s five levels from prevention through limiting consequences, the NRC phrase successive compensatory measures, and at least two diverse and independent shutdown systems where one alone can hold the reaction in check.
evidence.shows: The operative principle is independence under failure, not simply having several controls.
evidence.source: IAEA SSR-2/1 and NRC sources as attributed in the baseline

transition_in.carries_over: A safeguard may fail.
transition_in.introduces: The nuclear philosophy of independent layers designed around that possibility.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: AI systems can apply the layered principle across prevention, detection, damage control, mitigation and consequences.

evidence.what: Keep all five existing AI list items: prevent with constrained tools, least privilege and scope; catch early with validation, evaluation gates and anomaly detection; stop damage with sandboxes and human review; mitigate with limits, circuit breakers and rollback; limit consequences with logs, monitoring and incident response.
evidence.shows: Each layer has a different role so failure of a prompt or filter need not leave the system without another defense.

transition_in.carries_over: Independent nuclear safeguards back one another up.
transition_in.introduces: Concrete AI safeguards organized by the same failure-aware principle.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Defense in depth means designing the next layer to hold, rather than merely adding more filters.

evidence.what: Unchanged Figure 3 and defense-in-depth-layers.jpeg show a crack in one inner ring while the next ring holds, retaining all five defense labels and the caption.
evidence.shows: The layer that survives the failure expresses the independence principle the list should be used to implement.

transition_in.carries_over: The list gives five different safeguard roles.
transition_in.introduces: The design test that makes those roles a layered system.

flow.rationale: State the failure question, explain the existing nuclear evidence, map it to AI controls, and interpret the map as a test of independence. The AI list before that evidence would look like an arbitrary checklist rather than a response to failure.

evidence.what: The existing organizational questions ask who is accountable, which decisions remain human, how work is reviewed, and how failures are caught and fixed.

transition_in.introduces: The organization’s operating model around AI.

evidence.what: Keep the existing comparison to institutions, norms, laws and accountability; retain the hedge It is fair to say before the historical nuclear statement and the list of regulation, operating discipline, liability, oversight and public trust.
evidence.shows: The social plant comparison concerns governance and operating conditions, not a new historical measurement or a claim about equal hazards.

transition_in.carries_over: Organizations need operating structures around capability.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The wider comparison concerns surrounding structure, not equivalence between AI danger and fission.

evidence.shows: The argument is about durable, trustworthy production use and surrounding work, not identical hazards, stable model physics or the absence of standalone model value.

conclusion.so_what: A team should plan, fund and own that surrounding work from the start instead of treating a convincing model demonstration as almost-finished production delivery.

non_goals.topic: A nuclear engineering tutorial or a safety-record debate about nuclear power.
A claim that AI is as physically dangerous as fission, or that it can melt down or detonate in any literal sense.
An AI-safety / x-risk policy argument. The control-plane point is about engineering and operating reality, not existential risk.

decision_log.decision: Chose the title AI Is the Reactor, Not the Plant to put the thesis in the title: the model is one part, the plant around it is the work.

Scope decided as both, layered: engineering control plane first, then widen to organization and society. Section: AI Software Development, next to the RISC and vibe-monolith posts. This preserves the legacy placement rationale as history; the journal contract now gives the exact reading order.

Nuclear depth kept light and accurate: a few verifiable touchpoints (heat source, control rods, three barriers, defense-in-depth, cost split) used as anchors, not a point-by-point engineering mapping, to keep the article readable and avoid over-stretching.
Will include an explicit Where the analogy breaks section, because the strongest version of an analogy names its own limits.
Decided NOT to use the ~80% of overnight cost is EPC figure: it was adversarially refuted in research (1-2). Use only the WNA cost-by-activity split and the attributed 1980 DOE breakdown.

Decided to scope the uncontrolled = dangerous point to powerful and useless without control, not explodes like a bomb, because low-enriched commercial reactors cannot detonate and real accidents are decay-heat/meltdown-driven over hours. Preserved as the legacy research decision, not a new verification in this pass.

Copy journal intent, acceptance criteria, the five thesis fields and role unchanged. Add six local supporting claims, but add no acceptance criteria or numeric word limit. The legacy spec set no numeric cap.
